newsitem.title: USA: Vote underscores city's sharp racial divisions.
newsitem.headline: Vote underscores city's sharp racial divisions.

text.p: The election of a Cuban-American to the second most powerful political office in Florida was credited Wednesday to a strong appeal on racial lines, an appeal that highlighted a wide racial divide in the Miami area.

Alex Penelas, a 34-year-old Democrat, defeated African-American Republican Arthur Teele, 50, by 60 percent to 40 percent Tuesday to become the mayor of Dade County in balloting that saw voters cross party lines to sticking close to racial allegiances.

Election officials estimated that 95 percent of Dade County's overwhelmingly Democratic black voters backed the Republican Teele. And 92 percent of Hispanic voters, most of them traditionally Republican Cuban-Americans, backed Penelas.
Non-Hispanic white voters, known in Miami as "Anglos," were about evenly divided, with 52 percent behind Penelas and 48 percent supporting Teele.

The voting followed a campaign where the two candidates pledged to avoid racial appeals, but their supporters did not. Such campaigning came to a head Tuesday, as some of Miami's black and Cuban radio stations aired virtually nonstop appeals that each ethnic group do its best to outvote the other.

One Spanish-language radio station asked Cubans to address "a problem with race" in voting. And a black station alluded to a "master plan by Cubans" to take over Dade County and warned that Spanish might become the area's official language if Penelas were elected.

Listeners seemed to respond, with a strong 52 percent turnout by Hispanic voters credited with Penelas's victory. Forty-six percent of eligible black voters cast ballots, while fewer than 30 percent of Dade County's Anglos turned out.
Forty percent of Dade County's 805,261 registered voters are non-Hispanic whites, 20 percent are black and 38 percent are Hispanic, with 2 percent classified as "other."
Observers said the racially-charged campaign would only exacerbate ethic tensions in Dade County, especially between African- and Cuban-Americans.

"This wasn't the worst campaign in that regard in Dade's political history, but to the extent that there were these types of divisive appeals, often on ethnic radio stations, it is regrettable, and over the long term, the community pays a price for it," said Art Teitelbaum, southern area director of the Anti-Defamation League.

Hispanics, most of them Cuban and many of them relatively new immigrants, account for more than 55 percent of the county's population, while blacks are just 21.4 percent. Penelas, born in Dade County, is the son of Cuban immigrants.

And experts said Tuesday's sound defeat of an attractive, experienced candidate -- Teele was former chairman of the Dade County Commission and a Reagan administration official -- was especially disheartening to voters who have been feeling more marginalized by the region's growing Latin population.

"I think that ethnic relations are strained in Miami now, particularly because there's a sense among African-Americans and among white voters that we are being overwhelmed by a Hispanic political juggernaut and the Penelas-Teele race sort of confirmed that in people's mind," said Marvin Dunn, acting director of the African New World Studies at Florida International University.
